headline: Serbia's National Bird Makes a Stunning Comeback
meta_description: Eastern imperial eagles are thriving in Serbia, with 29 breeding pairs recorded in the country's most successful conservation year since 2017.
summary_short: Serbia's national bird is experiencing a banner year. Twenty-nine breeding pairs of eastern imperial eagles were counted, with 16 pairs successfully raising 25 chicks to…
body:
Serbia's eastern imperial eagle—the majestic bird emblazoned on the nation's flag—is experiencing its most successful breeding year since targeted conservation efforts began in 2017. Researchers counted 29 breeding pairs across the country, with 16 of those pairs successfully raising 25 chicks to fledging age. The milestone marks a dramatic recovery from just seven years ago, when only a single breeding pair remained in the country. The Serbian Bird Protection and Research Society (DZPPS) documented the achievement, describing a population that has rebounded from the brink of local extinction.

Most sightings have clustered in the Banat region along the Tisa River, though the eagles' range is expanding. For the first time, researchers found a nesting couple in southern Bačka, and the recovery has been bolstered by recolonization from neighboring Hungary. To track the population's movements and dispersal patterns, young fledglings will be fitted with radio transceivers when safe to do so—a method that will reveal where these eagles hunt, travel, and establish themselves across the continent.

The turnaround echoes successful conservation efforts elsewhere in Europe. White-tailed eagles have recently returned to Belgium for the first time in 500 years, while France has doubled its eagle mating pairs through decades of dedicated work. Milan Ružić, Executive Director of DZPPS, has described the eastern imperial eagle as "a symbol of nature conservation in Serbia," noting that growing public interest in the bird's recovery offers genuine reason for optimism. Listed as "Vulnerable" by the IUCN, the species remains endangered across much of Eurasia, making Serbia's comeback a beacon for what sustained protection can achieve.
